title: Strange Cases of the Mind · Episode 1
chapters: Phineas Gage: the man with an iron rod through his head
Sleep paralysis: the demon on your chest
Deja vu and other glitches of memory

units.t: Strange Cases of the Mind. Episode one.
In this episode: Phineas Gage: the man with an iron rod through his head, Sleep paralysis: the demon on your chest and Deja vu and other glitches of memory.
Part one. Phineas Gage: the man with an iron rod through his head.
In 1848 a metre-long iron bar shot clean through a young man's skull, and he lived.
What happened to his personality afterwards became one of the most retold, and most exaggerated, stories in psychology.
Rod through the skull.
On 13 September 1848, Phineas Gage, a 25-year-old railway foreman near Cavendish, Vermont, was packing gunpowder into a drilled hole with a tamping iron.
Something went wrong, possibly because the sand had not yet been added.
The powder ignited and fired the rod upward like a spear.
It was about 1.
1 metres long, more than 3 centimetres thick and weighed around six kilograms.
It entered under his left cheekbone, passed behind his left eye and burst out through the top of his skull.
Astonishingly, Gage was speaking within minutes and rode to town sitting upright in an ox cart.
The physician John Martyn Harlow kept him alive through a dangerous infection, and by early 1849 Gage was walking about.
'No longer Gage'.
Before the accident, Harlow wrote, Gage had been a shrewd, energetic and well balanced worker, the most efficient foreman his employers had.
Afterwards he was 'fitful, irreverent', impatient of advice and full of plans he abandoned as quickly as he made them.
Friends said he was 'no longer Gage', and his employers would not take him back.
Harlow's report, published in full in 1868, became a landmark.
It suggested that parts of the brain at the front of the head have something to do with personality, judgement and self control, not just with movement or the senses.
For a young science of the brain, it was dramatic evidence.
How the story grew.
Here is where the story goes wrong.
Harlow's notes were fairly brief, and Gage left no account of his own.
Into that gap, later writers poured colour.
In books and lectures Gage became a drunk, a brawler, a wife beater, a drifter who could never hold a job.
Almost none of this is supported by evidence.
Gage was never married, and there is no good record of heavy drinking or violence.
He did spend a short time showing himself and his iron to paying audiences.
The exaggerations tended to grow whenever someone needed a vivid example of the frontal lobes going wrong.
The forgotten recovery.
The Australian psychologist Malcolm Macmillan spent decades tracking down every scrap of evidence about Gage.
In the early 1850s Gage went to Chile, where for roughly seven years he drove a coach between Valparaíso and Santiago.
That is a demanding job: handling a team of horses on rough mountain roads, keeping to a schedule and dealing with passengers.
Macmillan argued that Gage's changes were probably most severe in the first months, and that he then rebuilt a working life, perhaps helped by a job with clear routines.
In 2009 two collectors identified the first known photograph of Gage, showing a well-dressed man proudly holding his iron.
What Gage really teaches.
In poor health, Gage left Chile in 1859 to join his family in San Francisco.
He began having epileptic seizures, very likely a late consequence of his injury, and died in May 1860, aged 36.
His skull and tamping iron are now in Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum.
Most scans suggest the damage was concentrated in the left frontal lobe.
Later cases confirmed that this region helps us plan, hold back impulses and behave appropriately with others.
The second lesson is quieter: a single dramatic case is easy to bend into whatever shape a writer needs.
The real Gage changed for a time, then appears to have recovered far more than most retellings admit.
The key idea: In 1848 an explosion drove an iron rod through Phineas Gage's head, and he survived.
Part two. Sleep paralysis: the demon on your chest.
You wake in the dark, unable to move, and you are certain someone is in the room.
For centuries people blamed witches and demons.
The real explanation lies in a brief mix-up between sleep and waking.
A terrifying few minutes.
Sleep paralysis usually happens as you fall asleep or wake.
You are aware of your surroundings and can usually open your eyes, but you cannot move your arms, legs or head, and may struggle to speak.
Episodes last from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, though they can feel much longer.

What makes many episodes frightening is what comes with them: a powerful sense that someone is in the room, pressure on the chest, and sometimes vivid sights, sounds or the sensation of being touched.
Then it ends.
It is more common than people think.
A widely cited 2011 review by Brian Sharpless and Jacques Barber estimated that about 8 per cent of people have had at least one episode, though estimates vary.
Stuck between two states.
The explanation lies in rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, the stage when most vivid dreaming happens.
During REM sleep, the brain actively switches off most of the body's voluntary muscles, leaving only the eyes and breathing muscles working.
This is protective, because it stops you acting out your dreams.
Normally the switch flips back the moment you wake.
In sleep paralysis, the transition goes slightly wrong.
Your conscious mind comes online while the muscle shutdown of REM is still in force.
You are, in effect, partly awake and partly still in a dreaming state, which is why the experience feels so real and so strange.
Demons, hags and ghosts.
If part of your brain is still in dream mode, dream imagery can spill into what you perceive with your eyes open.
That is why people see shadowy figures, hear footsteps or feel hands upon them.
The sense of threat may be sharpened because the brain's alarm systems are active during REM.
The weight on the chest may be partly because breathing is automatic and shallow in REM, so a deliberate deep breath is hard.
Because the experience is so similar everywhere, many cultures have their own explanations.
In Newfoundland it is being 'hagged'.
In Japan it is kanashibari, roughly 'bound in metal'.
The word nightmare originally meant a 'mare', a spirit that sat on sleepers.
Henry Fuseli's 1781 painting The Nightmare shows a demon on a sleeping woman's chest.
What makes it more likely.
Perhaps the most important factors are not getting enough sleep and having an irregular sleep schedule.
That is one reason shift workers, new parents, students during exams and long haul travellers can be more prone to it.
Stress and anxiety appear to raise the risk, and it is more common among people with post traumatic stress disorder.
Some studies suggest sleeping on your back may make episodes more likely, though the evidence is limited.
Frequent sleep paralysis can also be one feature of narcolepsy, a sleep disorder that causes overwhelming daytime sleepiness.
For most people, though, an occasional episode is simply a harmless glitch.
Riding it out.
Simply understanding sleep paralysis can take away much of its power.
Many people find that reminding themselves 'this is sleep paralysis, it is harmless and it will pass' makes episodes far less frightening.
Some find that focusing on slow breathing, or trying to move something small such as a finger or toe, helps break the spell, although evidence for specific techniques is limited.
Over the longer term, the most useful steps are getting enough sleep and keeping a regular sleep routine where possible.
If episodes are frequent or distressing, or come with extreme sleepiness during the day, talk to a GP, who may refer you to a sleep specialist.
The key idea: Sleep paralysis is being awake but unable to move, often with a sense of a presence in the room.
Part three. Deja vu and other glitches of memory.
That eerie sense that you've lived this exact moment before.
Is it a glimpse of the future, a past life, or something stranger and more ordinary?
Familiar but false.
You walk into a cafe you have never visited, and everything feels oddly known: the light, the clatter of cups, the conversation next door.
For a few seconds you feel certain you have lived this moment, while knowing you can't have.
The French phrase means 'already seen'.
Surveys suggest roughly two thirds of people have experienced it.
It is most common in teenagers and young adults, becomes less frequent with age, and has been linked with tiredness and stress.
What makes it special is the clash: part of your mind says 'I know this' while another says 'no, you don't'.
Psychologist Chris Moulin argues this clash is the heart of the experience.
Forgotten layouts.
Psychologist Anne Cleary at Colorado State University proposed that deja vu can occur when a new scene resembles something in your past that you can't consciously recall.
In virtual reality experiments, new scenes with a similar spatial layout to earlier ones were more likely to trigger deja vu when people could not recall the earlier scene.
That unfamiliar cafe may share its arrangement of tables, windows and counter with a room you forgot years ago.
Many people also feel they can predict what comes next.
In a 2018 test, participants felt sure which way to turn, but their predictions were no better than chance.
The premonition is a feeling, not foresight.
The brain checks itself.
Researchers can trigger something like deja vu in the lab.
People hear related words such as bed, pillow, night and dream, but never the word sleep.
Asked if they heard a word starting with 's', they know they did not, yet 'sleep' feels oddly familiar.
In a study presented in 2016, Akira O'Connor and colleagues scanned brains during these moments.
Activity showed up mainly in frontal areas involved in decision-making and conflict, rather than in the memory hubs.
One interpretation is that deja vu reflects the brain checking its memories for errors.
If so, it may be a sign of a healthy memory system doing its job.
When it's a medical clue.
For most people, deja vu is harmless and occasional.
It does have a known link with temporal lobe epilepsy, where some people experience intense deja vu as an aura, a warning sensation at the start of a seizure.
Surgeons stimulating parts of the temporal lobe during operations have also triggered deja vu-like feelings, which helped researchers pin down where the sensation arises.
Signs that it might need checking include happening very often, lasting a long time, or coming with blank spells, strange smells or tastes, or confusion.
This is general information rather than medical advice.
If you are concerned, talk to your GP.
healthdirect also has information.
Jamais vu and its cousins.
Deja vu has a stranger opposite called jamais vu, 'never seen': the sense that something you know well, such as a familiar word or face, suddenly seems foreign.
You can trigger a version by writing a common word like 'door' over and over until it looks wrong.
In 2023, Chris Moulin, Akira O'Connor and colleagues won an Ig Nobel Prize, the award for research that first makes people laugh and then think, for studying this.
Another familiar glitch is the tip-of-the-tongue state, when you are sure you know a name but can't retrieve it, often recalling its first letter or number of syllables.
Together, these quirks reveal memory as a busy, self-monitoring process, not a simple recording.
The key idea: Deja vu is a strong sense of familiarity combined with the awareness that it is wrong.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was remarkable about Gage's accident?
Answer. He survived and was talking within minutes.
Question two. What is sleep paralysis?
Answer. Being awake but briefly unable to move, often with hallucinations.
Question three. What distinguishes deja vu from an ordinary false memory?
Answer. You feel familiarity while knowing it can't be right.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
